scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

For our family wedding, we were all expected to purchase matching fabric so we could attend in coordinated outfits. Would you have bought the fabric?

I can’t make purchasing decisions for you, but I can certainly help you weigh the pros and cons of buying matching fabric for a family wedding! Here’s a balanced perspective to consider: ### **Potential Benefits:** 1. **Unity & Tradition** – If the wedding has a strong family tradition of coordinated outfits (e.g., bridesmaids, groomsmen, or even extended family), it can feel meaningful and symbolic. 2. **Photography** – Matching fabrics can create cohesive, visually striking photos, especially if everyone is wearing complementary colors or patterns. 3. **Ease of Coordination** – If you’re not great at matching outfits, this ensures everyone looks intentional and put-together. 4. **Sentimental Value** – Some families cherish the idea of "matching" as a way to honor the couple or create a shared memory. ### **Potential Drawbacks:** 1. **Cost** – Buying fabric (especially high-quality or custom-made) can be expensive, especially if multiple people are involved. Sewing or altering clothes may also add to the expense. 2. **Limited Style** – Matching fabrics might restrict individuality, making outfits feel less personal or comfortable. 3. **Logistics** – Coordinating measurements, patterns, and sewing timelines can be stressful, especially if people have different body types or preferences. 4. **Wearability** – If the fabric is formal (e.g., heavy satin or stiff brocade), it might not be comfortable for all-day wear or movement. 5. **Alternative Ideas** – Instead of full matching, you could: - Choose a **shared color palette** (e.g., everyone wears a shade of blue or gold). - Opt for **similar silhouettes** (e.g., all dresses with the same neckline or pants with matching details). - Use **accessories** (e.g., coordinated scarves, shoes, or jewelry) for a subtle touch. ### **Questions to Ask Yourself:** - **Is this a family expectation or tradition?** If it’s deeply meaningful, it might be worth it. - **How much flexibility do you have in styling?** Could you mix fabrics or patterns in a way that feels intentional? - **What’s the budget?** Could you compromise (e.g., matching shoes or bags instead of full outfits)? - **How do you feel about uniformity vs. individuality?** Would you prefer to stand out or blend in? ### **Alternative Compromises:** - **Group Outfit:** Only the immediate bridal party matches (e.g., bridesmaids + groomsmen in coordinated pieces). - **Themed Accessories:** Everyone wears the same color shoes or a specific piece (like a belt or clutch). - **Fabric Swap:** If you love the idea of matching but not the full commitment, you could buy a small piece (like a scarf or pocket square) to tie things together. Would you like help brainstorming specific outfit ideas based on the wedding’s theme or your personal style? Or would you prefer tips on negotiating the expectation with your family?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: This is a **1**—**not** AITA, but there’s room for nuance and growth in how you handle this. ### **Why Not AITA?** 1. **Setting Boundaries is Healthy** – You’ve made it clear you’re not comfortable with car maintenance beyond basic tasks, and that’s reasonable. You’re not obligated to learn advanced mechanics just because she owns a car. 2. **You’ve Already Taught Her** – You bought her a PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. If she refuses to learn, that’s on her—not you. 3. **Gender Roles Are Outdated** – Her belief that car care is "a man’s job" is problematic, and you’re right to call it out. However, **how** you call it out matters. 4. **You’re Not the Problem** – She’s the one refusing to take responsibility for her own car, not you. Her reliance on strangers (and her dismissive attitude toward learning) is the real issue. ### **Where You Could Improve** 1. **You’re Not the "Rescuer"** – While you’re not obligated to fix her car, **passively refusing** (without offering *any* help) might come across as punitive rather than firm. Instead of saying *"I won’t do it,"* try: - *"I won’t pump your tire, but if you ever want to learn, I’ll show you again."* - *"If you don’t fix this, you’ll risk getting stranded. That’s on you, not me."* - *"I’m not your mechanic. Figure it out yourself—or pay someone to do it."* 2. **She’s Testing Your Limits** – She’s pushing because she knows you’ll cave (or because she’s used to men "taking care" of her). **Stay firm.** If she keeps asking, you can say: - *"I’ve already shown you how. If you don’t want to learn, that’s your choice, but I won’t keep doing it for you."* - *"If you want this fixed, pay for it yourself."* 3. **Her "Male Friends" Are Wrong** – The fact that other men agree with her is **not** an excuse. Real men don’t enable dependency—they encourage self-sufficiency. If she’s surrounded by men who think this is normal, she’s not with the right people. ### **Final Verdict: 1 (Not AITA, but could be better)** - **You’re not obligated** to fix her car, and you’re right to refuse. - **But you could handle it with more dignity**—don’t make it a power struggle, just **stop enabling her helplessness**. - **If she keeps relying on strangers**, that’s her problem, not yours. Would you like help drafting a firm but polite response for next time she asks?
